title: Trustee education should avoid ATO modules
full_text:
The SMSF Association has cautioned the government about adopting the ATO’s education modules as the basis for its proposed mandatory trustee education at the time of a new fund’s establishment, pointing out they were developed for a different purpose.
The professional body stated that last week association chief executive Peter Burgess, head of policy and advocacy Tracey Scotchbrook and head of professional standards Keddie Waller met with Assistant Treasurer and Financial Services Minister Daniel Mulino and Treasury to discuss proposals to strengthen consumer protections for individuals establishing new SMSFs.
“We discussed the government’s proposal to introduce mandatory trustee education before registration. It was clear from these discussions that this proposal is still very much in its infancy,” it stated in an update sent to members today.
“At this early stage, it appears the ATO is being considered as the sole provider of the mandatory education.
“In its impact analysis, Treasury noted that the ATO has existing education modules that could be leveraged. We raised concerns about this approach and explained our strong preference that the ATO not be the only provider.
“Importantly, the ATO’s existing modules were designed for a different purpose – as an education direction following non-compliance.
“These modules necessarily have a strong regulatory and compliance focus, but they were not designed to help prospective trustees decide whether an SMSF is appropriate for them.”
The association added it offered assistance in the setting of the standards and outcomes for trustee education where it would support informed decision-making while not adding barriers to the establishment of a new fund, adding it was also important to correctly set the timing and content of the material.
“If its purpose is to help consumers make an informed decision about whether an SMSF is right for them, it needs to occur early enough in the establishment process to inform that decision, rather than after they have already committed to establishing a fund,” the update stated.
“Reflecting the Minister’s comments at the National Press Club that it will be ‘basic education’, the standards should not imply that every new trustee requires detailed technical competency across the entire SMSF life cycle.
“Rather, the education should provide prospective trustees with sufficient understanding of their roles and responsibilities and the knowledge needed to make an informed decision about whether an SMSF is appropriate for them.
“For this reason, we believe the approximate three-hour time commitment referred to in Treasury’s impact analysis is excessive for achieving this stated purpose.”
author: Jason Spits
heading: Superannuation and Investments
